title: More: Mode-Optimized Reasoning with Self-Adaptive Effort for Self-Evolving Agents

Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence

Title:More: Mode-Optimized Reasoning with Self-Adaptive Effort for Self-Evolving Agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Self-evolving training improves the performance of agents on difficult tasks through verifiable feedback, but it often applies costly deliberation uniformly across tasks. To address this problem, we propose Mode-Optimized Reasoning with Self-Adaptive Effort (MORE), a self-evolving training framework that adaptively selects both reasoning form and computational effort for each task. Specifically, MORE follows a two-stage training paradigm: (i) \emph{Stage 1} establishes a compact prior over direct answering, short and long chain-of-thought, and code-based reasoning, and (ii) \emph{Stage 2} self-evolves this prior with Mode-Adaptive and Test-time Effort PPO (MATE-PPO) on generated, verifiable task streams without curated data. By learning mode selection and token expenditure jointly, MORE allocates concise reasoning to tasks that permit it while retaining extended deliberation where it is useful. Across coding, mathematics, and general-reasoning benchmarks, MORE achieves consistent performance gains on Base and Coder backbones at model scales from 3B to 14B. During inference, MORE demonstrates higher accuracy and better efficiency, with markedly shorter response lengths and reduced inference time.

report.summary: MORE is a self-evolving training framework that adapts reasoning mode and computational effort per task, improving accuracy and efficiency for 3B-14B agents.
report.background: Self-evolving agents are increasingly trained with reinforcement learning and verifiable feedback, allowing them to improve on coding, math, and general reasoning tasks without heavy human labeling. However, many current methods apply long chain-of-thought deliberation uniformly, even when a direct answer or short reasoning would suffice. That wastes inference compute, increases latency, and raises serving costs. At the same time, test-time scaling has made reasoning effort a key design variable: models can spend more tokens on hard problems but should avoid overspending on easy ones. MORE addresses this by learning both the form of reasoning and the amount of effort each task needs, rather than treating deliberation as a fixed setting. The work fits a broader industry push toward adaptive, cost-aware agents that can self-improve from generated task streams.
key_points: MORE uses a two-stage training paradigm. Stage 1 builds a compact prior over four reasoning modes: direct answering, short chain-of-thought, long chain-of-thought, and code-based reasoning. Stage 2 then self-evolves this prior with Mode-Adaptive and Test-time Effort PPO, called MATE-PPO, on generated verifiable tasks without curated data.

The framework jointly learns which reasoning mode to use and how many tokens to spend. This lets it allocate concise reasoning to tasks that permit it while retaining extended deliberation where useful. In practice, the model can choose code-based reasoning for some coding tasks and shorter natural-language reasoning for simpler problems.

Across coding, mathematics, and general-reasoning benchmarks, MORE reports consistent gains on Base and Coder backbones from 3B to 14B parameters. At inference, it shows higher accuracy and better efficiency, with markedly shorter response lengths and reduced inference time compared with uniform-deliberation baselines.

A key claim is scalability without curated training data: MORE self-evolves on generated, verifiable task streams. That reduces reliance on hand-built datasets and aligns with the idea of agents improving through feedback loops. However, the abstract reports benchmark results rather than broad deployment evidence, so reproducibility and real-world robustness remain open questions.
report.impact: MORE points toward a more cost-aware generation of AI agents. For the AI industry, adaptively choosing reasoning mode and token budget could lower serving costs and make test-time compute more economically viable. For developers, the framework suggests that agent training should optimize a policy over reasoning strategies, not just final answers, and that PPO-style self-evolution can be paired with mode selection. This may influence RL infrastructure, evaluation, and inference routing. For regular users, the practical benefit is faster, cheaper agents that still deliberate on hard problems, though gains depend on reliable verification signals and may vary outside benchmark settings. The main caveat is that adaptive effort must not silently reduce accuracy on tasks that only appear easy.
report.tools: Watch for the authors' code release on arXiv or GitHub. Related open-source tools include verl, OpenRLHF, and Hugging Face TRL for PPO and self-evolving RL; vLLM and SGLang for efficient inference and latency measurement; lm-evaluation-harness for benchmark comparisons; and OpenHands or SWE-agent for coding-agent evaluation. These can help reproduce mode-adaptive effort and compare accuracy, response length, and inference cost.
